theme: The Temple dedicated; Solomon’s great prayer
readingInstruction: Read 1 Kings 8:1-66. This is the dedication of the temple, and Solomon’s great prayer. Read the prayer slowly, and notice how often he asks God to hear and forgive.
settingTheScene: The temple is complete, and the ark is brought in. The glory of the LORD fills the house in a cloud, as it filled the tabernacle in Exodus 40. Solomon blesses the people and offers a long prayer of dedication. He asks God to hear the prayers offered toward the temple, whatever the circumstances, and to forgive. The feast ends with enormous sacrifices and joy.
observation: The priests bring the ark into the Most Holy Place, “and when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD” (8:6-10).
“For the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (8:11).
“The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. I have built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever” (8:12-13).
“O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart” (8:23).
“But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (8:27).
“Hear in heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive” (8:30).
“For there is no one who does not sin” (8:46).
“That all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other” (8:60).
interpretation:
The cloud that fills the temple is a sign that God has accepted the house. It echoes the glory at Sinai and in the wilderness tabernacle. The priests cannot stand to minister. The reality of God’s presence overwhelms them. This is the high point of the temple’s history. It is the moment when the dream of God dwelling with his people seemed to come true.

Solomon’s prayer is a masterpiece of theology. It starts with praise: there is no God like you, who keeps covenant and shows steadfast love. It acknowledges that God has kept his promise to David. And then comes the great honesty of verse 27: “Will God indeed dwell on the earth? Heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house.” Solomon knows that the temple does not limit God. It is a place where God chooses to put his name, not a box that holds him.

The heart of the prayer is a series of seven situations: wrong done between neighbors, defeat in war, drought, famine and plague, the foreigner who comes, battle, and exile. In each, Solomon asks God to hear in heaven and forgive. The temple becomes a house of prayer. The assumption throughout is that the people will sin: “There is no one who does not sin.” The temple, then, is above all a place of forgiveness. It is where sacrifice is offered, where sins are atoned, and where the lost may turn back.

Verses 41 to 43 are a remarkable window: the foreigner who comes from a far country “for your name’s sake” is to be heard, “that all the peoples of the earth may know your name.” The temple was meant to be a light to the nations.

The dedication ends with a benediction and a feast of fellowship offerings. “The people went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.”
connection: Jesus is the true dwelling of God, the glory in the flesh (John 1:14). He is greater than the temple (Matthew 12:6). On the cross, the temple curtain was torn, opening the way into the presence of God (Matthew 27:51; Hebrews 10:19-22). He called the temple “a house of prayer for all nations” (Mark 11:17). Acts 2 shows the Spirit filling the church, as the glory once filled the house.
application:
Pray the pattern of Solomon’s prayer: praise, honest confession, and a request for forgiveness.

Remember that God cannot be contained by any building. Where do you try to confine him?

Pray for someone from another nation to come to know the name of the LORD.
prayerPrompts: Praise God that heaven cannot contain him and yet he dwells with his people.
Tell him what you want him to hear and forgive.
